text: Support's page leads with a trend. Finance's page, built this lesson, leads with a number instead, because Finance's real question is how much are we refunding, right now, this week.

A headline card, bound to total_refund_amount, formatted as currency using Power BI's own column formatting — no DAX needed, since the Snowflake view already returns a clean numeric value. A trend chart beside it, refund_week by total_refund_amount, the same shape as Support's chart, reading from a completely different table.

Here's the deliberate part: refund_event_count gets its own card, right beside the dollar total, not buried in a table somewhere. It was built into the view back in Lesson 8 specifically as a sanity check, and putting it visibly on the page means anyone looking at this report has a real chance of noticing if that count ever looks structurally wrong. A subscriber slicer rounds out the page, for drilling into one account specifically.

One honest note before moving on. This page, built exactly as described, is correct. It accurately reflects whatever is in refund_events at the moment Power BI refreshes. That's worth sitting with: a report page being built correctly doesn't guarantee the data feeding it is correct.
Both pages are built. Next lesson is where that gap stops being theoretical: a real report comes in that the numbers don't match.
